issues.legal_issue: Material impairment of a rented building’s value or utility is assessed from the landlord’s perspective and may be inferred from proved effects of a tenant’s acts.
material_facts: The tenant constructed a wall in a verandah and installed a door without the landlord’s consent.
The construction stopped the flow of light and air, and the tenant removed fixtures.
The lower courts found that the construction materially affected the value or utility of the building.
issues.conclusion: The proved effects permitted the courts to infer material impairment from the landlord’s perspective, without requiring separate direct evidence from the landlord of the resulting loss in value or utility.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, acts likely to materially impair a building’s value or utility can justify eviction. Impairment is assessed from the landlord’s perspective and is an inferential fact that may be deduced from proved facts. Om Parkash v. Amar Singh, concerning material alteration under a different statute, did not assist on these facts.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_made_structural_change and change_obstructed_light_or_air and change_removed_fixtures

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.tenant_made_structural_change: The tenant made a structural change to the rented premises.
predicates.change_obstructed_light_or_air: The structural change obstructed the flow of light or air in the building.
predicates.change_removed_fixtures: The tenant removed fixtures from the premises.
predicates.material_impairment_may_be_inferred: The building’s material loss of value or utility may be inferred from the proved effects of the tenant’s acts, assessed from the landlord’s perspective.

issues.definition: When a tenant’s structural change obstructs light or air and is accompanied by removal of fixtures in a rent-control eviction proceeding, the change’s proved effects may support an inference of material impairment.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not disturb concurrent factual findings supported by proved facts merely by re-evaluating the evidence in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found that the tenant had constructed the wall and installed the door and that the construction materially affected the building’s value or utility.
The Appellate Authority and High Court confirmed those findings.
The Supreme Court considered the challenge in an appeal by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding was a finding of fact supported by the evidence, and the Court would not re-evaluate the evidence and set it aside.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not re-evaluate evidence to upset a concurrent finding of fact supported by proved facts.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_supported_by_proved_facts: The factual finding rests on facts proved in the proceeding.
predicates.supreme_court_does_not_reweigh_evidence_: The Supreme Court does not re-evaluate evidence to set aside the supported concurrent factual findings.

issues.definition: In an appeal by special leave, supported factual findings made consistently by the courts below are not set aside through re-evaluation of the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: When a tenant seeks to avoid eviction despite proof of acts likely to impair a building’s value or utility, the tenant must plead and prove circumstances against eviction before the landlord must rebut them and the Rent Controller weighs the competing circumstances.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found that the tenant had committed acts that materially affected the building’s value or utility.
The tenant did not plead or prove circumstances showing that eviction should nevertheless be refused.
issues.conclusion: The Rent Controller was not at fault for failing to exercise discretion to refuse eviction because the tenant had made no attempt to establish circumstances against eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 gives the Rent Controller discretion to order eviction, unlike the mandatory direction applicable to cases under Section 13(3). Where the tenant seeks to show that eviction is unwarranted despite the statutory ground being established, the tenant must first plead and prove relevant circumstances; the burden then shifts to the landlord to rebut them, after which the Rent Controller weighs the circumstances.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_established: The Rent Controller finds that the tenant’s acts satisfy the ground for eviction.
predicates.tenant_did_not_prove_circumstances_again: The tenant did not plead and prove circumstances showing that eviction should nevertheless be refused.
predicates.no_error_in_ordering_eviction_without_re: The Rent Controller commits no error by ordering eviction without refusing the landlord’s relief.

issues.definition: Where the eviction ground is established in a rent-control proceeding, the Rent Controller commits no error by ordering eviction if the tenant has not proved circumstances against it.
